original_question: (A. Glutsyuk, S. Tabachnikov ) Given two nested closed convex hypersurfaces, assume that the billiard transformations on the set of oriented lines that intersect both hypersurfaces commute. Prove that the hypersurfaces are confocal ellipsoids.
target_in_paper: Problem 4.12 in §4.2.2 ("Geometry of caustics, invariant surfaces and commuting billiard maps"); the same statement appears as Problem 3.12 in the arXiv v1 PDF with page numbers. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's official formulation almost verbatim: it has the correct attribution to A. Glutsyuk and S. Tabachnikov, the correct hypothesis of two nested closed convex hypersurfaces with commuting billiard transformations on the oriented lines intersecting both, and the correct conclusion that the hypersurfaces must be confocal ellipsoids. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))
missing_details: The paper places this problem in the Euclidean higher-dimensional setting, namely as the case of dimensions greater than 2; elliptic and hyperbolic analogues are mentioned only afterward as separate analogues, not as part of the main statement. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))

For a stand-alone formulation, one should specify that each hypersurface defines a billiard reflection map on the common phase space of oriented lines intersecting both hypersurfaces. The section's general billiard setup defines billiard maps exactly this way. ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))

The meaning of "commute" should be made explicit as equality of compositions of the two reflection maps on their common domain: B1∘B2 = B2∘B1. This is implicit in the paper's wording but not spelled out in the draft. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))

Some regularity sufficient to define billiard reflection is implicit from the section setup: the billiard discussion starts with smooth strictly convex boundaries and says the higher-dimensional extension is immediate, whereas Problem 4.12 itself uses the shorter phrase "closed convex hypersurfaces." ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))

The draft does not indicate the paper's contextual status of the statement: it is posed as an open problem/converse in higher dimensions, after the paper notes that the planar converse had already been proved and that confocal ellipsoids do yield commuting billiard transformations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))
refined_question: Let Σ1, Σ2 ⊂ ℝ^d, with d ≥ 3, be nested closed convex hypersurfaces, with enough regularity for each Σi to define a billiard reflection map Bi on the common phase space ℒ of oriented lines intersecting both Σ1 and Σ2. Assume that B1 and B2 commute on ℒ, i.e. B1∘B2 = B2∘B1. Prove that Σ1 and Σ2 are confocal ellipsoids. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))
justification: This is the exact open problem stated in the paper, and your draft is already extremely close to the official wording. The surrounding paragraph identifies it as the higher-dimensional converse to the known commuting property for confocal ellipsoids, after recalling the already-solved planar converse and before separately mentioning constant-curvature analogues. The earlier billiards setup in the same section supplies the implicit meaning of the billiard transformations as reflection maps on the phase space of oriented lines. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))
